questions.prompt: How does currying transform a function?
questions.explanation: The curry function checks if it has received all required arguments (`fn.length` = 3). If not, it returns a new function collecting more args. All three call patterns eventually pass 3 args (1+2+3=6). Currying enables **partial application** and building specialized functions from general ones.

questions.title: What does immutability via `map` produce compared to direct mutation?
questions.prompt: What does immutability via `map` produce compared to direct mutation?
questions.explanation: `mutated = original` creates an alias (same reference). `mutated[0].val = 99` mutates `original[0].val` to `99`. `immutable` spreads each item into a new object, so `original[0].val` is `99` at map time → `99 * 2 = 198`. The `immutable` array contains new objects, not references to originals.

questions.title: What does a `transducer` pattern achieve?
questions.prompt: What does a `transducer` pattern achieve?
questions.explanation: Both produce the same result: even numbers squared. The `reduce` approach is a transducer-style single pass — no intermediate array created. `filter().map()` creates an intermediate array. For large datasets, single-pass is more memory-efficient. Both produce `[4, 16, 36, 64, 100]` and have the same length.

questions.title: What is memoization and what does this memoize function produce?
questions.prompt: What is memoization and what does this memoize function produce?
questions.explanation: Memoization caches results by input. First `expensiveFn(5)` — cache miss, calls fn, `callCount=1`. Second `expensiveFn(5)` — cache hit, returns cached `25`, `callCount` unchanged. `expensiveFn(6)` — cache miss, calls fn, `callCount=2`. Only 2 actual function calls despite 3 invocations.

questions.title: What does a point-free style function produce?
questions.prompt: What does a point-free style function produce?
questions.explanation: Words with length > 3: `"hello"` (5), `"world"` (5) pass. `"foo"` (3), `"bar"` (3), `"baz"` (3) fail (not strictly greater than 3). Both approaches use the same predicate logic and produce the same result. `longerThan(3)` is a curried predicate factory — `longerThan(3)` returns `word => word.length > 3`.

questions.title: What does a `flatMap` vs `map` + `flat` comparison show?
questions.prompt: What does a `flatMap` vs `map` + `flat` comparison show?
questions.explanation: `flatMap` is equivalent to `map` followed by `flat(1)`. Each sentence is split into an array (`["hello","world"]`, `["foo","bar"]`). `flatMap` flattens one level automatically. Both produce `["hello","world","foo","bar"]` with length 4. `flatMap` is slightly more efficient (single iteration).

questions.title: How does a lens pattern enable immutable deep property updates?
questions.prompt: How does a lens pattern enable immutable deep property updates?
questions.explanation: `setIn` recursively creates new objects at each level of the path — an immutable deep update (lens pattern). `state` is unchanged (`name` still `"Alice"`). `newState` is a new object tree where `name` is `"Bob"`. `state === newState` is `false` — they are different objects (immutable update). This pattern is fundamental in Redux reducers and functional state management.

questions.title: A developer uses class inheritance. What is the output?
questions.prompt: A developer uses class inheritance. What is the output?
questions.explanation: `super(color)` must be called before accessing `this` in a derived class constructor. `super.describe()` calls the parent method. `instanceof` walks the prototype chain, and `Circle` extends `Shape`, so `c instanceof Shape` is `true`.

questions.title: What does the static method example output?
questions.prompt: What does the static method example output?
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class itself, not instances. `MathHelper.add()` works; `m.add()` throws `TypeError`. Instance methods like `multiply` are accessible on the instance.

questions.title: What does `extends` and `super` do in class inheritance?
questions.prompt: What does `extends` and `super` do in class inheritance?

options.text: `TypeError` — private fields not accessible via super

questions.explanation: `super('Woof')` must be called in the subclass constructor before accessing `this`. `super.speak()` calls the parent\'s `speak()` method — which accesses `#sound` on the instance (`'Woof'`). Private fields are accessible within the class that defines them, so `speak()` can access `#sound`. `instanceof` checks the prototype chain → `true`.

questions.title: What do static class fields and methods belong to?
questions.prompt: What do static class fields and methods belong to?
questions.explanation: Static fields/methods belong to the **class**, not instances. After 3 `new Config()` calls, `Config.instances = 3`. Accessing a static field via an instance (`new Config('c').instances`) returns `undefined` — instances don\'t inherit static properties. `Config.reset()` sets `instances` back to `0`.

questions.title: What do private class fields protect against?
questions.prompt: What do private class fields protect against?
questions.explanation: Private class fields (`#field`) are a **syntax-level** restriction — accessing `#balance` outside the class body is a `SyntaxError` (caught at parse time, not runtime). The getter `balance` provides controlled public access. Private fields truly encapsulate data, unlike the `_convention` which is just a naming hint.

questions.title: What does abstract-like class behavior look like in JavaScript?
questions.prompt: What does abstract-like class behavior look like in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: `new.target` inside a constructor refers to the class being constructed. If `Shape` is instantiated directly, `new.target === Shape` → throw. If a subclass extends `Shape`, `new.target` is the subclass (`Circle`) → passes. `Circle` overrides `area()` → works correctly. This is JavaScript\'s pattern for abstract classes.

questions.title: How do class mixins compose behavior?
questions.prompt: How do class mixins compose behavior?
questions.explanation: Mixins are functions that take a base class and return an extended class. Composing `Serializable(Validatable(Entity))` creates a class that has methods from all three. `u` has `name` and `age` (2 keys) → `validate()` returns `true`. `serialize()` returns `JSON.stringify(u)` — a string. Mixins enable multiple-inheritance-like composition.

questions.title: What does `Symbol.iterator` on a class produce?
questions.prompt: What does `Symbol.iterator` on a class produce?
questions.explanation: Implementing `[Symbol.iterator]()` makes the class iterable. The method returns an iterator object with a `next()` function. Spread syntax (`[...new Range(1, 4)]`) uses the iterator protocol. The iterator yields `1, 2, 3, 4` then signals `done: true`. This makes the class work with `for...of`, spread, destructuring, etc.

questions.title: What does class expression allow that class declaration doesn\'t?
questions.prompt: What does class expression allow that class declaration doesn\'t?
questions.explanation: Class expressions can be returned from functions, assigned to variables, or passed as values. Here, `createClass` is a factory that creates classes with closured `name`. Each generated class captures a different `name` via closure. This pattern enables dynamic class generation and is used in higher-order patterns.

questions.title: What does a class `getter`/`setter` pair do?
questions.prompt: What does a class `getter`/`setter` pair do?
questions.explanation: `new Temperature(0)` → `#celsius = 0`. `t.fahrenheit` getter: `0 * 9/5 + 32 = 32`. `t.fahrenheit = 212` setter: `#celsius = (212 - 32) * 5/9 = 100`. `t.celsius` getter returns `100`. Getters/setters let you expose derived/computed properties while maintaining encapsulation.

questions.title: What is the output when a subclass doesn\'t call `super()`?
questions.prompt: What is the output when a subclass doesn\'t call `super()`?
questions.explanation: In a derived class, `this` is not available until `super()` is called. Accessing `this` before `super()` throws a `ReferenceError`. After `super()` is called, `this` is available. `this.x = 1` is set by `Base` constructor. `this.y` was never assigned (the assignment threw) → `undefined`. So `"After super: 1 undefined"`.

questions.title: A project uses ES Modules. Which statement is correct about the following import?
questions.prompt: A project uses ES Modules. Which statement is correct about the following import?

options.text: This throws a `SyntaxError` — you cannot mix default and named imports
`add` is the default export; `PI` and `multiply` are named exports — this is valid
`add` will be `undefined` because default exports must use curly braces

questions.explanation: ES Modules allow one default export and multiple named exports per file. Default imports have no curly braces; named imports use `{ }`. Combining both in one import statement is perfectly valid.

questions.title: What is the difference between named and default exports for tree-shaking?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between named and default exports for tree-shaking?

options.text: Default exports are always tree-shaken; named exports never are
Named exports are statically analyzable and enable better tree-shaking; default exports that export objects can prevent tree-shaking

questions.explanation: Bundlers (webpack, Rollup) perform tree-shaking by analyzing static imports. Named exports (`export const fn`) allow bundlers to know exactly which exports are used and eliminate unused ones. Default exports that export objects (`export default { fn1, fn2 }`) prevent tree-shaking because the whole object must be imported. Use named exports for utility functions to enable effective tree-shaking.

questions.title: What does dynamic `import()` enable that static `import` doesn\'t?
questions.prompt: What does dynamic `import()` enable that static `import` doesn\'t?

options.text: Dynamic `import()` is a Promise-based expression that enables lazy/conditional loading of modules
Dynamic imports cannot be used with named exports
Dynamic imports are not supported in Node.js

questions.explanation: `import()` is an async function that returns a Promise resolving to the module\'s namespace object. It enables: code splitting (only load what\'s needed), conditional imports, lazy loading on user interaction, and runtime path determination. Static imports are hoisted and always loaded — dynamic imports are flexible runtime operations.

questions.title: What does circular module dependency cause?
questions.prompt: What does circular module dependency cause?

options.text: One of them will log `undefined` due to the circular dependency — the import is a live binding but may not be initialized yet
Module system throws an error and refuses to load

questions.explanation: ES Modules handle circular imports with **live bindings** — the binding exists but may be `undefined` at first execution. `b.js` imports `a` from `a.js`, but `a.js` hasn\'t finished evaluating yet → `a` is `undefined` when `b.js` logs it. Circular dependencies are legal but can cause subtle initialization order bugs. Avoid them or restructure shared code into a third module.

questions.title: What is module scope in ES Modules?
questions.prompt: What is module scope in ES Modules?

options.text: `0` — each import creates a fresh module instance
`2` — both imports share the same module singleton

questions.explanation: ES Modules are **singletons** — a module is evaluated once and cached. All imports of the same module share the same instance. Both `increment` and `inc2` reference the same function that closes over the same `count` variable. Two `increment()` calls → `count = 2`.

questions.title: What does `import * as` create?
questions.prompt: What does `import * as` create?
questions.explanation: `import * as utils` creates a **namespace object** containing all exports. Named exports are accessible as properties (`utils.PI`, `utils.square`). The default export is accessible as `utils.default`. The namespace object is **live** — if the module updates an exported variable, the namespace object reflects the update.

questions.title: What does `export { x as y }` enable?
questions.prompt: What does `export { x as y }` enable?

options.text: `SyntaxError` — internal functions cannot be exported with aliases

questions.explanation: `export { name as alias }` re-exports a binding under a different name. This is the **renaming export** syntax — useful for keeping internal implementation names private while providing a cleaner public API. Consumers use `add` and `multiply` without knowing the internal naming convention.

questions.title: How does `import.meta` provide module context?
questions.prompt: How does `import.meta` provide module context?
questions.explanation: `import.meta` is a meta-property available in ES Modules. `import.meta.url` is always a string — the URL/path of the current module (set by the runtime). `import.meta.env` is injected by bundlers like Vite/webpack for environment variables — not available in plain Node.js. `import.meta` properties are host-defined, so they vary by environment.

questions.title: What is the difference between ES Modules and CommonJS?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between ES Modules and CommonJS?

options.text: ES Modules are static and synchronous; CommonJS is dynamic and asynchronous
ES Modules use `import/export` (static, async-friendly, tree-shakeable); CommonJS uses `require/module.exports` (dynamic, synchronous, not tree-shakeable)
They are interchangeable with no practical differences

questions.explanation: Key differences: ESM uses `import/export` (static, hoisted, live bindings, async loading, tree-shakeable). CJS uses `require()` (dynamic, synchronous, cached, returns snapshot). ESM\'s static structure enables tree-shaking and better optimization. CJS\'s `require()` can be used conditionally or in loops. Node.js supports both, but they have interop nuances.

questions.title: What does re-exporting from a module enable?
questions.prompt: What does re-exporting from a module enable?

options.text: `SyntaxError` — barrel files are not allowed in ES Modules
A barrel/index file that aggregates exports, providing a single import point for consumers
All re-exported modules are loaded eagerly regardless of usage

questions.explanation: Re-exporting (`export { X } from './X.js'`) creates **barrel files** that aggregate multiple module exports. Consumers import from a single path instead of knowing the internal file structure. `export * from` re-exports all named exports. `export { default as Input }` re-exports a default export as a named export. Barrel files improve API ergonomics but can hurt tree-shaking if implemented poorly.

questions.title: A developer makes a GET request using `fetch()`. The server returns a 404 status. What is the behavior of the returned Promise?
questions.prompt: A developer makes a GET request using `fetch()`. The server returns a 404 status. What is the behavior of the returned Promise?

options.text: The Promise rejects because 404 is an error status
The Promise resolves with `response.ok === false` and `response.status === 404`
The Promise resolves with `response.ok === true` — 404 is a valid HTTP response

questions.explanation: `fetch()` only rejects its Promise for **network failures** (DNS resolution failure, no connection, etc.) — not for HTTP error status codes. A 404 or 500 response is still a valid HTTP response, so the Promise resolves. Always check `response.ok` (true for status 200â€“299) or `response.status` to detect HTTP errors explicitly.

questions.title: What is the correct pattern for making a `fetch` call and reading the JSON response?
questions.prompt: What is the correct pattern for making a `fetch` call and reading the JSON response?

options.text: This is incorrect — `response.json()` is synchronous and does not need `await`
This correctly handles both network errors and HTTP status errors, and properly reads the JSON body
Calling `throw` inside an `async` function causes an unhandled rejection

questions.explanation: `response.json()` returns a **Promise** that resolves to the parsed JSON body — it must be `await`ed. Checking `response.ok` before calling `.json()` is the correct pattern to distinguish HTTP errors (which `fetch` resolves) from successful responses. The `throw` inside an `async` function returns a rejected Promise, which callers can `catch`.

questions.title: How do you send a POST request with a JSON body using `fetch()`?
questions.prompt: How do you send a POST request with a JSON body using `fetch()`?

options.text: This is incorrect — `fetch` only supports GET requests natively
The `body` should be a plain object, not a JSON string
This correctly sends a POST request with a JSON-serialized body and proper Content-Type header
`Content-Type` header is automatically set by `fetch` and should not be specified manually

questions.explanation: To send JSON, you must: 1) set `method: 'POST'`, 2) set `Content-Type: application/json` header (tells the server how to parse the body), and 3) `JSON.stringify` the object (the `body` must be a string, `Blob`, or `FormData` — not a plain object). Omitting `JSON.stringify` sends `"[object Object]"` as the body.

questions.title: What happens if you call `response.json()` twice on the same response?
questions.prompt: What happens if you call `response.json()` twice on the same response?

options.text: Returns the same parsed object twice — the body is cached after the first call
Throws `TypeError: body stream is locked` (or `body used already`) — response bodies can only be consumed once
Makes a new network request to re-fetch the data

questions.explanation: The `Response` body is a readable stream that can only be consumed **once**. After `response.json()` (or `response.text()`, `response.blob()`) is called, the body stream is fully read and cannot be read again. If you need to use the body multiple times, call `response.clone()` before reading: `const clone = response.clone()`.

questions.title: What is the difference between `response.json()`, `response.text()`, and `response.blob()`?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between `response.json()`, `response.text()`, and `response.blob()`?

options.text: All three return Promises: `json()` parses the body as JSON, `text()` returns a raw string, `blob()` returns binary data as a `Blob`
`text()` automatically parses JSON if the response has `Content-Type: application/json`
`blob()` is only available in Node.js, not in browsers

questions.explanation: All response body reading methods return Promises and consume the body stream. Use `json()` for API responses returning JSON. Use `text()` for HTML, CSV, or plain text. Use `blob()` for images, audio, or file downloads. Use `arrayBuffer()` for low-level binary manipulation. Choose based on the `Content-Type` of the response.

questions.title: How do you send authentication headers and cancel a long-running `fetch` request?
questions.prompt: How do you send authentication headers and cancel a long-running `fetch` request?

options.text: `Authorization` headers cannot be set from JavaScript due to browser security restrictions
This correctly attaches a bearer token and implements a 5-second timeout using `AbortController`
`controller.abort()` cancels the Promise but the network request continues

questions.explanation: `AbortController` and its `signal` allow cancelling a `fetch` request. When `abort()` is called, the Promise rejects with an `AbortError`. This pattern combines: auth header attachment, a 5-second timeout using `setTimeout`, and cleanup with `clearTimeout` on success. `AbortController` actually cancels the underlying network request, not just the Promise.

questions.title: How do you run multiple `fetch` requests in parallel and handle all results?
questions.prompt: How do you run multiple `fetch` requests in parallel and handle all results?

options.text: The three `fetch` calls run sequentially — `Promise.all` waits for the first before starting the next
This runs all three requests in parallel and resolves when all complete; rejects if any fails
`Promise.all` with `fetch` always rejects because network requests are unreliable
This is equivalent to three sequential `await fetch(...)` calls

questions.explanation: `Promise.all` starts all Promises simultaneously — all three `fetch` calls are initiated at once. If the user, posts, and comments APIs each take 200ms, sequential awaits would take ~600ms total; `Promise.all` takes ~200ms. If any request fails, `Promise.all` rejects immediately. Use `Promise.allSettled` if partial failure is acceptable.

questions.title: What is the key difference between `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` for error handling?
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` for error handling?

options.text: `fetch` automatically handles HTTP error codes; `XMLHttpRequest` requires manual checking
Both APIs reject/error for HTTP error status codes (4xx, 5xx)
`fetch` requires explicit `response.ok` checking for HTTP errors; `XMLHttpRequest` uses separate `onload`/`onerror` events; both need HTTP status checks
`XMLHttpRequest` is deprecated and should never be used

questions.explanation: Both APIs require manual HTTP status checking. `fetch` is Promise-based (cleaner with `async/await`), supports streaming, and has a modern API. `XMLHttpRequest` is callback-based, uses events (`onload`, `onerror`, `onprogress`), and is more verbose. Neither automatically throws for HTTP error codes — developers must check `response.ok` (fetch) or `xhr.status` (XHR). `fetch` is preferred in modern code.

questions.title: What is the correct order of events when JavaScript starts executing a program?
questions.prompt: What is the correct order of events when JavaScript starts executing a program?

options.text: Functions are executed immediately when declared; variables are set up last
1) Global Execution Context is created (hoisting: `name = undefined`, `greet` = function); 2) Code runs line by line; 3) `greet()` creates a new Function Execution Context pushed onto the Call Stack
The Call Stack processes items from a queue (FIFO), not a stack
Each line creates its own separate execution context

questions.explanation: JavaScript execution has two phases per context: **Creation Phase** (variables hoisted as `undefined`, function declarations fully hoisted, `this` bound) and **Execution Phase** (code runs line by line). When a function is called, a new Execution Context is pushed onto the Call Stack. When it returns, it is popped off. The Global Execution Context remains until the program ends.

questions.title: What does the Call Stack look like at the moment `c()` runs?
questions.prompt: What does the Call Stack look like at the moment `c()` runs?

options.text: `[c]` — only the currently executing function is on the stack
`[Global, a, b, c]` — each nested call adds a frame; on return each is popped in reverse order
`[a, b, c, Global]` — the last-called function is at the bottom
`[Global]` — functions only appear on the stack after they return

questions.explanation: The Call Stack is a LIFO (Last In, First Out) data structure. Global is always the base. `a()` is called → pushed. `a` calls `b` → pushed. `b` calls `c` → pushed. At the peak: `[Global, a, b, c]`. `c` returns → popped. `b` returns → popped. `a` returns → popped. This is why it's called a "stack" and why deeply nested calls can cause stack overflows.

questions.title: What causes `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`?
questions.prompt: What causes `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`?

options.text: Using too much heap memory for variables inside the function
Each `countdown` call pushes a new frame onto the Call Stack without ever popping; the stack overflows when its size limit is reached
`console.log` inside a recursive function causes a stack overflow
The event loop queue fills up and blocks new tasks

questions.explanation: Every function call consumes a Call Stack frame. Without a base case, `countdown` calls itself infinitely. Each call adds a frame; none return to be popped. Eventually the engine's stack size limit (typically ~10,000â€“15,000 frames) is hit, throwing `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. Fix: add a base case (`if (n <= 0) return`) or convert to iteration / use `setTimeout` for very deep recursion.

questions.title: What does the JavaScript engine do during the **creation phase** of an execution context?
questions.prompt: What does the JavaScript engine do during the **creation phase** of an execution context?

options.text: Throws `ReferenceError` for both — nothing is set up before code runs
`undefined`, `ReferenceError` — `var` is hoisted and initialized to `undefined`; `let` is hoisted but stays in the TDZ (uninitialized)
`1`, `2` — all declarations are fully initialized in the creation phase

questions.explanation: During the **creation phase**, the engine: 1) creates the Variable Environment (`var` → `undefined`, function declarations → full function), 2) creates the Lexical Environment (`let`/`const` → hoisted but **uninitialized** in TDZ), 3) binds `this`. Only during the **execution phase** are values assigned. Accessing a `let` variable before its declaration line (while still in the TDZ) throws `ReferenceError`.

questions.title: What does the scope chain in an execution context determine?
questions.prompt: What does the scope chain in an execution context determine?

options.text: `"global"` — functions always look up to the global scope first
`"outer"` — the scope chain walks from inner's context → outer's context → global; `x = 'outer'` is found first
`ReferenceError` — `x` is not in `inner`'s own execution context
`undefined` — `x` in outer is not accessible to inner

questions.explanation: The **scope chain** is built when a function is defined (lexical scoping). When `inner()` runs, its execution context has a reference to the outer function's environment (where `x = 'outer'`), and that has a reference to the global environment (where `x = 'global'`). Variable lookup walks inward-to-outward and stops at the first match. This chain is created at definition time, not at call time.

questions.title: A developer wants to prevent excessive API calls while typing in a search box. Which technique is correct?
questions.prompt: A developer wants to prevent excessive API calls while typing in a search box. Which technique is correct?

options.text: This is throttling — it limits calls to one per interval
This is debouncing — it waits for inactivity before calling the function
This is memoization — it caches the result of the function
This creates a memory leak because `timer` is never cleared

questions.explanation: Debouncing delays function execution until after a period of inactivity. Each call resets the timer. Throttling would cap calls to a maximum frequency. Memoization caches results. `clearTimeout` prevents the memory leak.

questions.title: A developer memoizes an expensive computation. What is the output and how many times is the heavy computation run?
questions.prompt: A developer memoizes an expensive computation. What is the output and how many times is the heavy computation run?
questions.explanation: First call `heavy(4)` — cache miss, computes `16`, stores it. Second call `heavy(4)` — cache hit, returns `16` without calling the function. `heavy(5)` — cache miss, computes `25`. Only 2 actual computations occur.

questions.title: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?

options.text: Debounce delays execution until after a pause; throttle limits execution to once per interval
Throttle delays execution until after a pause; debounce limits execution to once per interval
Both are identical — just different naming conventions
Debounce is for mouse events; throttle is for keyboard events

questions.explanation: **Debounce**: delays function until after `delay` ms of silence (no new calls). Use for search input (wait until user stops typing). **Throttle**: ensures function runs at most once per `interval` ms regardless of call frequency. Use for scroll/resize handlers. Rule of thumb: debounce = "wait for quiet time"; throttle = "rate-limit".

questions.title: What does `requestAnimationFrame` do for smooth animations?
questions.prompt: What does `requestAnimationFrame` do for smooth animations?

options.text: `requestAnimationFrame` syncs DOM updates with the browser\'s repaint cycle (~60fps), preventing jank
`requestAnimationFrame` is slower — it adds an extra 16ms delay

questions.explanation: `requestAnimationFrame` schedules the callback just before the browser\'s next repaint. Unlike `setTimeout(fn, 16)` (which drifts and can miss frames), `rAF` is synchronized with the display refresh rate. The browser can also batch/optimize `rAF` callbacks and pause them in background tabs to save power.

questions.title: What does DocumentFragment do for DOM performance?
questions.prompt: What does DocumentFragment do for DOM performance?

options.text: Both approaches cause the same number of reflows
`DocumentFragment` batches all nodes and triggers a single reflow/repaint on insertion
`appendChild` is always batched automatically by the browser

questions.explanation: Each `appendChild` to a live DOM element can trigger reflow/repaint. `DocumentFragment` is an off-screen container — nodes added to it don\'t trigger reflows. When the fragment is appended to the DOM, all its children are inserted in one operation — a single reflow/repaint. For 1000 items, this is a significant performance gain.

questions.title: What is the key performance benefit of virtual DOM?
questions.prompt: What is the key performance benefit of virtual DOM?

options.text: Virtual DOM is faster than real DOM for every operation
Virtual DOM minimizes expensive real DOM operations by computing the minimal diff (reconciliation) needed and applying only those changes in batch
Virtual DOM stores data in memory, avoiding network requests
Virtual DOM is only useful for server-side rendering

questions.explanation: Direct DOM manipulation is expensive (triggers reflow/repaint). Virtual DOM frameworks (React, Vue) maintain an in-memory representation of the DOM. When state changes, a new virtual DOM is computed and **diffed** against the previous one. Only the minimal set of actual DOM changes is applied. For frequent updates, this batching approach can significantly reduce layout thrashing.

questions.title: What does code splitting enable in large applications?
questions.prompt: What does code splitting enable in large applications?

options.text: Splitting code into multiple files that are all loaded upfront
Dividing the bundle into smaller chunks that are loaded on demand, reducing initial load time
Splitting CSS from JavaScript for parallel loading
Minifying JavaScript to reduce file size

questions.explanation: Code splitting (via `import()`, webpack, Rollup) divides the app into chunks. Only the initial chunk loads at startup; other chunks load when needed (route change, user interaction). This reduces Time to First Byte (TTFB) and Time to Interactive (TTI). Combined with lazy loading and route-based splitting, it dramatically improves perceived performance for large SPAs.

questions.title: What is the performance impact of memory leaks in JavaScript?
questions.prompt: What is the performance impact of memory leaks in JavaScript?

options.text: No impact — JavaScript\'s garbage collector handles all memory management
Memory usage grows indefinitely, eventually causing slowdowns, tab crashes, or OOM errors
The garbage collector detects and fixes the leak automatically
Memory leaks only affect mobile browsers

questions.explanation: A memory leak occurs when objects that are no longer needed are still referenced (preventing garbage collection). Here, `cache` grows every 100ms with 1MB arrays. GC cannot collect them because `leaky` holds a closure reference. Over time: slowdowns → UI freezes → browser tab crash (OOM). Use Chrome DevTools Memory profiler to detect heap growth and leaked object retention.

questions.title: What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?
questions.prompt: What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?

options.text: Both approaches cause the same number of layout calculations
Interleaving reads/writes forces the browser to synchronously recalculate layout repeatedly; batching reads then writes allows a single calculation
`offsetHeight` is cached by the browser, so reads are free
CSS transitions eliminate layout thrashing automatically

questions.explanation: Layout properties (`offsetHeight`, `clientWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`, etc.) trigger a **synchronous layout calculation** to return an accurate value. If you write to the DOM first (invalidating layout) and then read, the browser is forced to recalculate layout synchronously. Batching all reads first (letting the browser defer layout) then writing avoids this expensive forced synchronous layout.

questions.title: What does `WeakRef` help with in performance-sensitive code?
questions.prompt: What does `WeakRef` help with in performance-sensitive code?

options.text: `WeakRef` holds a weak reference — the object can be collected; `deref()` returns `undefined` after collection
`WeakRef` is not supported in modern browsers
Setting `obj = null` creates a strong reference via `WeakRef`

questions.explanation: `WeakRef` allows you to hold a reference to an object without preventing its garbage collection. `deref()` returns the object if it still exists, or `undefined` if collected. Useful for caches where you want to allow eviction under memory pressure. The GC timing is non-deterministic — the output could be either depending on GC activity.

questions.title: What does worker thread offloading solve?
questions.prompt: What does worker thread offloading solve?

options.text: Both approaches block the UI equally
Worker threads run in a separate thread — heavy computation doesn\'t block the main thread\'s UI rendering
Web Workers share memory with the main thread automatically
Worker threads are only available in Node.js

questions.explanation: JavaScript is single-threaded. `heavySync()` blocks the event loop — the UI freezes for the entire duration. Web Workers run in a separate OS thread with their own event loop. Communication is via `postMessage` (structured clone or transferable objects). The main thread remains responsive. Use Workers for image processing, encryption, data transformation, or any CPU-intensive work.

questions.title: A developer implements a Singleton. Is the following a correct Singleton pattern?
questions.prompt: A developer implements a Singleton. Is the following a correct Singleton pattern?

options.text: `false` — each `getInstance()` call creates a new object
`true` — this correctly implements the Singleton pattern

questions.explanation: The IIFE creates a private `instance` variable. `getInstance()` creates the instance only once (lazy initialization) and returns the same object on subsequent calls. `db1 === db2` is `true` because they reference the same object.

questions.title: A developer uses the Observer/Pub-Sub pattern. What is logged when this runs?
questions.prompt: A developer uses the Observer/Pub-Sub pattern. What is logged when this runs?
questions.explanation: Both listeners are registered for `"data"`. When `emit("data", 5)` is called, all registered listeners execute with `data = 5`. This is the Publish-Subscribe pattern used extensively in Node.js\'s `EventEmitter`.

questions.title: A developer implements a Factory pattern. What does this return?
questions.prompt: A developer implements a Factory pattern. What does this return?
questions.explanation: The Factory returns an object based on `type`. For `"square"` with `size = 4`, `area()` computes `4 ** 2 = 16`. The factory pattern decouples object creation from usage, making it easy to add new shapes.

questions.title: What problem does the Decorator pattern solve?
questions.prompt: What problem does the Decorator pattern solve?

options.text: It prevents the original `add` function from being called
It adds logging behavior to `add` without modifying its source — separating cross-cutting concerns
It creates a new function that replaces `add` permanently

questions.explanation: The Decorator pattern wraps a function/object to add behavior without modifying the original. `withLogging` is a higher-order function (decorator) that adds logging as a cross-cutting concern. The original `add` is unchanged and reusable. This pattern is the basis for TypeScript decorators, middleware, and aspect-oriented programming.

questions.title: How does the Strategy pattern improve code flexibility?
questions.prompt: How does the Strategy pattern improve code flexibility?

options.text: `TypeError` — functions cannot be stored in objects

questions.explanation: The Strategy pattern encapsulates interchangeable algorithms. The `Sorter` class delegates to a strategy function selected at runtime. Switching algorithms requires only changing the strategy, not the `Sorter` class. In real implementations, each strategy would have different algorithm implementations. Useful for payment processors, compression algorithms, validation rules, etc.

questions.title: What does the Command pattern enable beyond simple function calls?
questions.prompt: What does the Command pattern enable beyond simple function calls?

options.text: Commands are identical to function calls — no difference
The Command pattern encapsulates operations as objects, enabling queuing, undo/redo, logging, and remote execution
Commands prevent functions from throwing errors
Commands are only useful for UI event handling

questions.explanation: The Command pattern turns operations into first-class objects with `execute()` and optionally `undo()`. This enables: **undo/redo** (keep a history of commands); **queuing** (store commands for later execution); **logging** (serialize command history for debugging/audit); **remote execution** (send serialized commands across a network). Used in text editors, game engines, and transactional systems.

questions.title: How does the Proxy pattern add behavior without modifying the target?
questions.prompt: How does the Proxy pattern add behavior without modifying the target?
questions.explanation: `Proxy` wraps the target and intercepts operations. The `set` trap fires when attempting to write a property — here it throws. The `get` trap is not defined, so reads pass through to the target normally. This implements read-only objects without modifying the original. `e.message.includes('read-only')` → `true`.

questions.title: What is the Mediator pattern\'s role in decoupling components?
questions.prompt: What is the Mediator pattern\'s role in decoupling components?

options.text: The Mediator directly connects all components for direct communication
The Mediator centralizes inter-component communication — components don\'t talk to each other directly, reducing coupling
The Mediator is identical to the Observer/Pub-Sub pattern
The Mediator pattern is only useful for backend systems

questions.explanation: The Mediator acts as a hub. Components (colleagues) communicate through the mediator, not directly with each other. This reduces dependencies from O(nÂ²) (all-to-all) to O(n) (all-to-mediator). Examples: air traffic control (planes â†” tower â†” planes), chat rooms (users â†” server â†” users), React\'s lifting state up, Redux store. Contrast with Observer: Mediator has logic; Pub-Sub is passive.

questions.title: What does the Chain of Responsibility pattern accomplish?
questions.prompt: What does the Chain of Responsibility pattern accomplish?
questions.explanation: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides to process or pass forward. Request 1: `token=true` → passes auth → `rateOk=true` → passes rate limit → processed. Request 2: `token=false` → auth handler rejects → `"Unauthorized"`. Used in middleware pipelines (Express, Koa), validation chains, event handling.

questions.title: What does the Module Revealing pattern expose and hide?
questions.prompt: What does the Module Revealing pattern expose and hide?
questions.explanation: The Revealing Module Pattern uses an IIFE to create a private scope. `_count` is private — not exposed in the returned object. Only `increment`, `decrement`, `getCount` are public. `increment()` twice (→ 2), `decrement()` once (→ 1). `counter.getCount()` returns `1`. `counter._count` is `undefined` — the private variable is inaccessible from outside.

questions.title: What does the Template Method pattern enforce?
questions.prompt: What does the Template Method pattern enforce?
questions.explanation: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in the base class, letting subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall structure. `process()` is the template — it calls `parse` → `validate` → `format`. `CSVProcessor` overrides `parse` (split by comma) and `format` (trim). `validate` uses the default pass-through. Result: `["a","b","c"]`.

questions.prompt: A developer stores a JWT token for authentication. Which storage method is most secure and why?

options.text: `localStorage` — easy to access and persists across sessions
`sessionStorage` — cleared when the tab closes, harder to steal
An `HttpOnly` cookie — inaccessible to JavaScript, preventing XSS theft
A global JavaScript variable — stays in memory, not persisted to disk

questions.explanation: `HttpOnly` cookies cannot be accessed via `document.cookie` or any JavaScript, making them immune to XSS token theft. `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` are readable by any script on the page. Pair `HttpOnly` with `SameSite=Strict` and `Secure` flags for CSRF protection.

questions.title: A developer evaluates user-submitted code. What is the security risk?
questions.prompt: A developer evaluates user-submitted code. What is the security risk?

options.text: No risk — `eval` runs in a sandbox
`eval` executes arbitrary code, enabling data exfiltration, XSS, and code injection
`eval` is blocked by Content Security Policy automatically

questions.explanation: `eval` executes any JavaScript string with the same privileges as the page. An attacker can inject code to steal cookies, redirect users, or manipulate the DOM. Use `JSON.parse` for data or a math expression parser library instead of `eval`.

questions.title: What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and how is it mitigated in JavaScript apps?
questions.prompt: What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and how is it mitigated in JavaScript apps?

options.text: CSRF is an attack that injects scripts into a page; mitigated by escaping HTML output
CSRF tricks authenticated users into making unintended requests; mitigated by CSRF tokens, `SameSite` cookies, and checking `Origin`/`Referer` headers
CSRF is a network-level attack; JavaScript cannot mitigate it
CSRF only affects GET requests; POST requests are safe by default

questions.explanation: CSRF exploits that browsers automatically send cookies with cross-origin requests. An attacker\'s page can trigger a request to your API with the victim\'s session cookie. Mitigations: **CSRF tokens** (unique per-session/per-form, validated server-side); **`SameSite=Strict/Lax` cookies** (prevent cross-site cookie sending); **`Origin`/`Referer` header validation**. Modern SPAs using Authorization headers (Bearer tokens) in AJAX requests are naturally CSRF-resistant.

questions.title: What does Content Security Policy (CSP) prevent?
questions.prompt: What does Content Security Policy (CSP) prevent?

options.text: CSP prevents unauthorized script execution by defining trusted sources for content, mitigating XSS attacks
CSP prevents all network requests from the page
CSP only affects images and stylesheets, not scripts

questions.explanation: CSP is an HTTP response header (`Content-Security-Policy`) that tells browsers which content sources are trusted. `script-src 'self' https://cdn.trusted.com` allows scripts only from the same origin and the CDN. Inline scripts (`<script>` tags, `eval`, `onclick`) are blocked unless explicitly allowed. This limits the impact of XSS — even if an attacker injects a script tag, it can\'t execute if the source isn\'t whitelisted.

questions.title: What is prototype pollution and why is it dangerous?
questions.prompt: What is prototype pollution and why is it dangerous?

options.text: `true` — the prototype is polluted, affecting all plain objects

questions.explanation: Prototype pollution occurs when attacker-controlled data modifies `Object.prototype`. After `Object.assign({}, payload)`, `Object.prototype.isAdmin = true`. Every plain object inherits from `Object.prototype` → `{}.isAdmin` is `true`. This can bypass security checks like `if (user.isAdmin)`. Mitigate with: `JSON.parse` with a reviver filtering `__proto__`; using `Object.create(null)` for merge targets; input validation; or using `structuredClone`.

questions.title: What makes `innerHTML` dangerous and what is the safe alternative?
questions.prompt: What makes `innerHTML` dangerous and what is the safe alternative?

options.text: `innerHTML` is safe — browsers sanitize HTML automatically
`innerHTML` parses HTML and executes embedded scripts/event handlers, enabling XSS; `textContent` sets plain text without parsing
`textContent` is deprecated — use `innerHTML` with manual escaping

questions.explanation: `innerHTML` causes the browser to parse and render HTML, including executing `onerror`, `onload`, `<script>` etc. `textContent` sets raw text — special characters become literal text, not HTML. Always use `textContent` for displaying user-provided data. If you need to render trusted HTML, use the `DOMParser` API with sanitization, or a trusted library like DOMPurify.

questions.title: What is the Same-Origin Policy and when does CORS override it?
questions.prompt: What is the Same-Origin Policy and when does CORS override it?

options.text: Same-Origin Policy allows all cross-origin requests by default; CORS restricts them
Same-Origin Policy blocks cross-origin read access from JavaScript; CORS is a server-controlled mechanism to selectively allow cross-origin requests
Same-Origin Policy applies only to cookies; CORS only applies to images
CORS completely overrides Same-Origin Policy for all request types

questions.explanation: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) restricts JavaScript from reading responses from different origins (different protocol, domain, or port). CORS (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or specific origin) is a server response header that tells browsers it\'s safe to expose the response to the requesting origin. SOP is enforced by browsers; CORS is a browser-respected server permission mechanism. Servers must opt-in to cross-origin access.

questions.title: What security risk does `postMessage` without origin validation create?
questions.prompt: What security risk does `postMessage` without origin validation create?

options.text: No risk — `postMessage` only works between trusted windows
Any page can send a message and inject HTML if origin is not validated; also using `innerHTML` with the data creates XSS
`postMessage` requires user interaction — it can\'t be automated
The browser blocks `postMessage` from different origins automatically

questions.explanation: `postMessage` enables cross-origin communication, but any window can send a message. Without validating `event.origin`, a malicious page can send arbitrary data. Combined with `innerHTML`, it\'s a direct XSS vector. Always: 1) validate `event.origin` against the expected sender; 2) never use `innerHTML` with untrusted `event.data`.

questions.title: What is clickjacking and how is it prevented?
questions.prompt: What is clickjacking and how is it prevented?

options.text: Clickjacking is when a script steals click events; prevented by `stopPropagation()`
Clickjacking overlays a transparent iframe over a legitimate page to trick users into clicking on the hidden target; prevented by `X-Frame-Options` or CSP `frame-ancestors`
Clickjacking is a type of XSS attack; prevented by input sanitization

questions.explanation: Clickjacking embeds your site in a transparent `<iframe>` over a fake UI. A user clicks the fake button but actually clicks a button on your site (e.g., "Transfer Money"). Prevention: `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (don\'t embed in iframes at all) or CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'` (modern equivalent). React apps should include these headers at the server level.

questions.title: What does the `Subresource Integrity (SRI)` attribute prevent?
questions.prompt: What does the `Subresource Integrity (SRI)` attribute prevent?

content.value:
<script
  src="https://cdn.example.com/library.js"
  integrity="sha384-abc123..."
  crossorigin="anonymous"
></script>

options.text: SRI prevents the script from accessing DOM APIs
SRI verifies the fetched resource matches the expected hash — preventing modified/compromised CDN resources from executing
SRI only works with CSS files, not JavaScript
SRI prevents the script from making network requests

questions.explanation: SRI mitigates supply chain attacks — if a CDN is compromised and serves a modified script, the `integrity` hash won\'t match and the browser will block execution. The browser computes the hash of the downloaded resource and compares it to the `integrity` attribute. If they don\'t match, the script is not executed. Always use SRI with third-party CDN resources.

questions.title: What is the risk of storing JWT tokens in `localStorage`?
questions.prompt: What is the risk of storing JWT tokens in `localStorage`?

options.text: JWTs are automatically encrypted when stored in `localStorage`
JWTs in `localStorage` are accessible to any JavaScript on the page — vulnerable to XSS attacks that can steal the token and impersonate the user
JWTs in `localStorage` expire automatically after 1 hour
`localStorage` is encrypted by the browser, making JWT storage safe

questions.explanation: A token in `localStorage` is readable by any script on the page. If an XSS vulnerability exists, an attacker can run `localStorage.getItem('jwt')` and exfiltrate the token. Safer: store JWTs in `HttpOnly` cookies (not accessible to JavaScript). Tradeoff: HttpOnly cookies require CSRF protection. For SPAs, implement a layered approach: short-lived access tokens in memory + HttpOnly refresh token cookies.

questions.title: A developer reads a DOM property inside a loop. What is the performance problem?
questions.prompt: A developer reads a DOM property inside a loop. What is the performance problem?

options.text: Reading `offsetWidth` inside the write loop forces synchronous reflow (layout thrashing)

questions.explanation: Writing styles (invalidates layout) and then reading layout properties (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`) forces the browser to synchronously recalculate layout. The fix is to batch reads together and writes together, or use `requestAnimationFrame`.

questions.title: What triggers a repaint vs. a reflow?
questions.prompt: What triggers a repaint vs. a reflow?

options.text: Changing `color` or `background` triggers reflow; changing `width` triggers repaint
Changing geometric properties (`width`, `height`, `margin`) triggers reflow; changing visual properties (`color`, `background`) triggers repaint only
Both reflow and repaint are the same operation
Reflow only happens on page load; repaint happens on every DOM change

questions.explanation: A **reflow** (layout) recalculates element positions and sizes — it is expensive. A **repaint** just redraws pixels for visual changes without affecting layout — cheaper. Reflows always trigger a repaint, but not vice versa. Use CSS `transform` and `opacity` for animations as they can be composited on the GPU without triggering reflow.

questions.title: What is the Critical Rendering Path?
questions.prompt: What is the Critical Rendering Path?

options.text: The fastest route between a client and a server
The sequence of steps the browser takes to convert HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels on the screen
The order in which CSS selectors are matched

questions.explanation: The Critical Rendering Path: 1) Parse HTML → DOM. 2) Parse CSS → CSSOM. 3) Combine DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree. 4) Layout (calculate positions/sizes). 5) Paint (draw pixels). 6) Composite (GPU layers). Optimizing the CRP (inline critical CSS, defer non-critical JS, minimize render-blocking resources) reduces Time to First Paint and Time to Interactive.

questions.title: What does `will-change` CSS property do for performance?
questions.prompt: What does `will-change` CSS property do for performance?

options.text: `will-change` hints to the browser that the element will be transformed, enabling GPU compositing and avoiding repaints during animation
`will-change` is deprecated and has no effect in modern browsers
`will-change` forces the element to render synchronously

questions.explanation: `will-change: transform` tells the browser to promote the element to its own compositing layer in advance. During animation, the GPU handles the layer composite without triggering reflow/repaint. Use sparingly — every composited layer uses GPU memory. Don\'t apply it to everything; only elements with frequent transitions/animations that cause jank.

questions.title: What is the difference between `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` events for performance?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` events for performance?

options.text: They fire at the same time
`DOMContentLoaded` fires when HTML is parsed (no waiting for images/CSS); `load` fires when ALL resources (images, stylesheets, iframes) are loaded
`DOMContentLoaded` is deprecated; only `load` should be used
`load` fires first; `DOMContentLoaded` fires after all rendering is complete

questions.explanation: `DOMContentLoaded` is the right event to initialize JavaScript that only needs DOM structure. `load` is needed when you require computed sizes of images or iframes. For performance, minimize work in both event handlers. Most app initialization should be done as early as possible — even in `<script defer>` which fires after parsing but before `DOMContentLoaded`.

questions.title: What does `IntersectionObserver` enable for performance?
questions.prompt: What does `IntersectionObserver` enable for performance?

options.text: `IntersectionObserver` efficiently detects when elements enter/exit the viewport without scroll event listeners, enabling lazy loading
`IntersectionObserver` is equivalent to `getBoundingClientRect` in a scroll handler

questions.explanation: `IntersectionObserver` uses the browser\'s internal intersection detection — no scroll event listeners, no `getBoundingClientRect` polling. The browser batches notifications, firing callbacks asynchronously. This pattern for lazy loading images is highly performant: images load only when they scroll near the viewport, reducing initial load size dramatically.

questions.title: What is the browser\'s rendering pipeline and where can JavaScript cause jank?
questions.prompt: What is the browser\'s rendering pipeline and where can JavaScript cause jank?

options.text: JavaScript always causes jank — only CSS animations are smooth
JavaScript running during the 16ms rendering budget (for 60fps) blocks the browser\'s style/layout/paint cycle, causing dropped frames (jank)
JavaScript runs separately from rendering and never causes jank
Jank only occurs with CSS animations, not JavaScript

questions.explanation: At 60fps, the browser has ~16ms per frame. If JavaScript blocks the main thread longer than that, frames are dropped (jank). Solutions: use `requestAnimationFrame` for visual updates; move heavy computation to Web Workers; use `setTimeout(fn, 0)` to yield; break large tasks with `scheduler.yield()` (or `MessageChannel` patterns). The Performance panel in DevTools shows "Long Tasks" (>50ms).

questions.title: What does HTTP caching with `Cache-Control` headers do for web performance?
questions.prompt: What does HTTP caching with `Cache-Control` headers do for web performance?

options.text: `Cache-Control` headers tell browsers and CDNs how long to cache resources, reducing network requests and improving load speed on repeat visits
`Cache-Control` is a JavaScript API for controlling memory caches
`Cache-Control: no-cache` disables all caching including in-memory

questions.explanation: `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` caches a file for a year with no re-validation (use with content-hashed filenames). `Cache-Control: no-cache` allows caching but revalidates with the server. `no-store` prevents caching entirely. For JS bundles: use content hashing (`main.abc123.js`) + long max-age. For HTML: short max-age or no-cache.

questions.title: What does `preload` vs `prefetch` resource hint do?

Both are identical — `as` attribute determines priority

Using `preload` incorrectly (for resources not used on the page) wastes bandwidth. `prefetch` is ideal for code-split chunks of routes the user might navigate to next.

questions.title: What does the `Performance` API provide for measuring real user performance?
questions.prompt: What does the `Performance` API provide for measuring real user performance?

options.text: The Performance API provides high-resolution timing (microseconds) for measuring real user metrics like processing time, navigation timing, and resource loading
Performance marks are only visible in DevTools and not accessible via JavaScript

questions.explanation: The `Performance` API (`performance.now()`, `mark()`, `measure()`) provides high-resolution timestamps accurate to microseconds. It\'s the foundation for Real User Monitoring (RUM). `getEntriesByType('navigation')` gives page load timing; `getEntriesByType('resource')` shows resource load times. Combined with `PerformanceObserver`, you can track Core Web Vitals (LCP, FID, CLS) in real user sessions.

questions.title: A developer registers a Service Worker. What does the following do?

Registers a Service Worker that can intercept network requests and cache assets
Enables push notifications without user permission
Creates a shared worker accessible across all browser tabs

questions.title: A developer implements a Cache-First caching strategy. What does this mean?
questions.prompt: A developer implements a Cache-First caching strategy. What does this mean?

options.text: Always fetches from the network; never uses the cache
Returns cached response if available; falls back to network if not cached
Always uses the network and updates the cache in the background

questions.explanation: Cache-First prioritizes the cache for speed, making the app work offline or in low-network conditions. If the resource is not cached, it fetches from the network. Contrast with Network-First (tries network, falls back to cache) for frequently updated content.

questions.title: What are the three core requirements of a Progressive Web App?
questions.prompt: What are the three core requirements of a Progressive Web App?

options.text: A Web App Manifest, a Service Worker, and HTTPS
A Web App Manifest, IndexedDB, and push notifications

questions.explanation: The three PWA requirements: 1) **Web App Manifest** (`manifest.json`) — metadata for add-to-homescreen (name, icons, display mode). 2) **Service Worker** — enables offline capability, background sync, push notifications (requires HTTPS). 3) **HTTPS** — required by browsers for Service Workers (except `localhost`). Together these enable installability, offline support, and app-like experience.

questions.title: What does a Service Worker\'s `fetch` event intercept?
questions.prompt: What does a Service Worker\'s `fetch` event intercept?

options.text: All network requests from the controlled page — the SW can respond with cached data, modify requests, or pass through to the network
Only requests to the SW\'s own origin

questions.explanation: The `fetch` event fires for every network request from controlled pages (except navigations with `navigate` scope issues). `event.respondWith()` intercepts the request and provides a response. The Service Worker acts as a programmable network proxy, enabling caching strategies, offline support, and request transformation.

questions.title: What does the `beforeinstallprompt` event enable?
questions.prompt: What does the `beforeinstallprompt` event enable?

options.text: `beforeinstallprompt` fires when the user manually installs the PWA
`beforeinstallprompt` allows the app to defer and customize the browser\'s install prompt for the PWA

questions.explanation: By default, browsers show an install banner automatically. `e.preventDefault()` suppresses it, storing the event. The app can show a custom install button at the right moment (after meaningful interaction). `deferredPrompt.prompt()` shows the native browser install dialog. `userChoice` tells you if the user accepted. This pattern improves install conversion rates.

questions.title: What does a `display` mode of `standalone` in the Web App Manifest do?
questions.prompt: What does a `display` mode of `standalone` in the Web App Manifest do?

options.text: The app opens in a regular browser tab with the address bar
The app opens without browser UI chrome (no address bar, back/forward buttons) — appears like a native app
The app only works in fullscreen mode

questions.explanation: `display: standalone` removes browser chrome (address bar, navigation buttons) when launched from the homescreen. The app gets its own window, taskbar entry, and splash screen. `fullscreen` goes further (no OS chrome). `minimal-ui` keeps some navigation. `browser` is the default tab experience. Standalone is the most common choice for app-like PWAs.

questions.title: What does `Background Sync` enable in PWAs?
questions.prompt: What does `Background Sync` enable in PWAs?

options.text: Background Sync allows the app to run JavaScript continuously in the background
Background Sync enables deferred actions (form submissions, data sync) to be retried when the user regains connectivity
Background Sync syncs the app\'s state with a server every 30 seconds
Background Sync is equivalent to server-sent events

questions.explanation: Background Sync registers a sync event with the Service Worker. If the user submits a form offline, the action is queued. When connectivity is restored, the browser fires a `sync` event in the Service Worker, which then makes the deferred request. This ensures data isn\'t lost due to intermittent connectivity — critical for mobile-first applications.

questions.title: What makes an app "installable" as a PWA?
questions.prompt: What makes an app "installable" as a PWA?

options.text: Any HTTPS website is automatically installable
The app must be on HTTPS, have a valid Web App Manifest with required fields (name, icons, start_url, display), and have an active Service Worker that handles `fetch` events
The app must be built with React or Angular
Only apps with 100 Lighthouse score are installable

questions.explanation: Chrome\'s install criteria: 1) HTTPS. 2) Valid manifest with `name`/`short_name`, `icons` (192px + 512px), `start_url`, and `display`. 3) Registered Service Worker with a `fetch` handler. 4) Has not been dismissed by the user recently. Lighthouse PWA audit checks all these criteria and reports installability issues with specific fixes.

questions.title: What does `Stale-While-Revalidate` caching strategy accomplish in a PWA?
questions.prompt: What does `Stale-While-Revalidate` caching strategy accomplish in a PWA?

options.text: Returns stale data and deletes it; fetches fresh data only when explicitly requested
Returns the cached response immediately while fetching an update in the background to refresh the cache for the next request
Returns stale data permanently — never updates
Blocks rendering until fresh data is available

questions.explanation: Stale-While-Revalidate is optimal for non-critical, frequently changing resources (news feeds, social content). The user sees stale (but fast) content immediately. In the background, the Service Worker fetches the latest version and updates the cache — the next visit shows fresh content. This balances speed (serve cached) with freshness (update in background). Libraries like Workbox implement this easily.

The Push API allows servers to send messages to Service Workers even when the app is closed; Notifications API displays the OS-level notification
Push notifications require a native app wrapper
Push notifications can only be sent from the same origin

questions.explanation: Push works even when the browser is closed: the push service (browser vendor\'s) receives the server\'s message and wakes the Service Worker. `event.waitUntil` keeps the SW alive while showing the notification. The user must grant notification permission. The server sends pushes via the Web Push Protocol using VAPID keys. This enables PWAs to re-engage users like native apps.

questions.title: What does the `Service Worker` lifecycle look like for an update?
questions.prompt: What does the `Service Worker` lifecycle look like for an update?

options.text: New SW installs and activates immediately, replacing the old one
New SW installs while old SW controls the page; new SW waits until all tabs close (or `skipWaiting()` is called) before activating
New SW downloads but never activates unless the user manually refreshes
Service Workers cannot be updated — a new URL must be used

questions.explanation: SW update lifecycle: 1) Browser detects new SW file. 2) New SW **installs** (`install` event). 3) New SW enters **waiting** state (old SW still controls pages). 4) When all controlled tabs close, new SW **activates**. Use `self.skipWaiting()` in `install` + `clients.claim()` in `activate` to take control immediately (with caution — can cause version mismatches).

questions.title: What is the output of these type coercion expressions?

questions.explanation: `+` is left-to-right: `1 + "2"` → `"12"` (string concat), then `"12" + 3` → `"123"`. `1 + 2` → `3` (numeric), then `3 + "3"` → `"33"`. `-` coerces to number: `"5" - 3 = 2`. `*` coerces both: `5 * 2 = 10`. `true + true` → `1 + 1 = 2`, then `2 + "1"` → `"21"`. Rule: `+` with any string = concatenation; `-`, `*`, `/` always coerce to numbers.

questions.title: What is the output of these array and object coercion expressions?

questions.explanation: `[] + []`: both arrays coerce to `""` (empty string via `.toString()`) → `""`. `[] + {}`: `[]` → `""`, `{}` → `"[object Object]"` → `"[object Object]"`. `{} + []` in expression context (not as a statement): `{}` is an empty object → `"[object Object]"`, `[]` → `""` → `"[object Object]"`. `+[]`: unary `+` converts `[]` → `""` → `0`. `+{}`: `{}` → `NaN`. These are notorious JavaScript gotchas.

questions.title: What is the output of these loose equality edge cases?
questions.prompt: What is the output of these loose equality edge cases?
questions.explanation: `null == undefined` → `true` (special spec rule: they are only equal to each other). `null == 0` → `false` (null only equals `undefined` with `==`). `null == false` → `false` (same rule). `NaN == NaN` → `false` (NaN is never equal to anything, even itself). Use `Number.isNaN(x)` to detect NaN, and `=== undefined` only for `undefined` checks.

questions.title: Which approaches correctly remove duplicate values from an array?

options.text: Approaches A and D are equivalent; B and C also work but are less efficient
Only Approaches A and B work
All four produce `[1, 2, 3, 4]` but with different time complexities

For primitives, use `[...new Set(arr)]` or `Array.from(new Set(arr))`. For objects (deduplicating by property), use `reduce` with a `Map`. questions.title: What does the following debounce implementation output when `search` is called rapidly?

Logs immediately: `"Searching: java"` — debounce removes all delays
Logs twice: first and last calls only

Since all four calls happen within 100ms of each other (well under the 300ms delay), earlier timers are continuously cancelled. Only after 300ms of no new calls does the last timer fire, logging `"Searching: java"`. This is ideal for search-as-you-type to reduce API calls.

questions.title: What does `Promise.resolve` and `async/await` output in this mixed synchronous/asynchronous scenario?
questions.prompt: What does `Promise.resolve` and `async/await` output in this mixed synchronous/asynchronous scenario?
questions.explanation: Synchronous: `"1"` → `asyncFunc()` runs synchronously until the first `await`: logs `"2"` → suspends at `await Promise.resolve()` → `Promise.resolve().then(...)` queues `"4"` as a microtask → logs `"5"`. Microtask queue: `await Promise.resolve()` inside `asyncFunc` resolves first (it was queued before the standalone `.then()`), but `"4"` was actually queued at the same tick as `asyncFunc`\'s continuation. Microtasks run in order: `await` continuation (logs `"3"`) runs after `"4"` — actually `"4"` resolves first because `asyncFunc`\'s inner `await` schedules a microtask, but the `.then(() => '4')` was enqueued after the `await`. Result: `"5"` → microtask `"4"` → microtask `"3"`.

questions.title: A Tech Lead reviews a PR with this error handling pattern. What is the issue?

questions.title: What is a circuit breaker pattern for async operations?

questions.title: What is the correct approach for managing long-polling vs Server-Sent Events vs WebSockets?

questions.title: How should a Tech Lead approach async state synchronization across multiple tabs?

questions.title: What is the right strategy for handling optimistic updates that fail?

Each module has a single, clear responsibility and can be tested, replaced, and evolved independently.

questions.title: What is the right strategy for managing shared utilities across micro-frontend teams?
questions.prompt: What is the right strategy for managing shared utilities across micro-frontend teams?

options.text: Each team should copy-paste shared utilities into their own codebase
Create an internal npm package (or monorepo package) for shared utilities, with semantic versioning, typed exports, and a documented upgrade path
Use a single global variable exposed on `window` to share utilities
Shared utilities should live in one team\'s repo and be imported directly via CDN

questions.explanation: Shared utilities across teams require: 1) **Versioned package** (npm/monorepo) — each team pins a version; breaking changes require a major version bump. 2) **TypeScript types** — consumer type safety. 3) **Documented API** — changelog, migration guides. 4) **Tree-shakeable** (ESM). Global variables (`window.utils`) create implicit coupling, version conflicts, and runtime errors. The internal package approach scales to N teams without coordination overhead.

questions.title: How should feature flags be architected for A/B testing at the module level?
questions.prompt: How should feature flags be architected for A/B testing at the module level?

options.text: Feature flags should be checked directly via inline `fetch` calls in each component
Feature flags are centralized, fetched once, and exposed as a module — components import flags without knowing the source, enabling easy testing and cleanup
Feature flags should only be implemented server-side
Using a module for feature flags prevents hot-reload from working

questions.explanation: Feature flag architecture: 1) Single source of truth (one fetch, one module). 2) Components import flags declaratively — no direct fetch calls scattered everywhere. 3) Easy to mock in tests (`jest.mock('./feature-flags', () => ({ newCheckout: true }))`). 4) Flags have clear naming and defaults. 5) Dead code elimination — when a flag is permanently enabled, remove the legacy branch. This scales from simple booleans to complex targeting rules.

questions.title: What is the benefit of the Domain-Driven Design (DDD) approach to module organization?
questions.prompt: What is the benefit of the Domain-Driven Design (DDD) approach to module organization?

options.text: DDD organizes code by technical layer: all controllers together, all services together, all models together
DDD organizes code by business domain: each domain (users, orders, payments) is self-contained with its own models, services, and UI components
DDD is only applicable to backend codebases
DDD eliminates the need for any shared utilities

questions.explanation: Layer-first organization (`/controllers`, `/services`, `/models`) requires changes to span multiple directories. Domain-first (`/users`, `/orders`, `/payments`) keeps related code co-located. Each domain exports a public API (facade pattern), hides internals, and can be owned by a team. This maps to micro-frontend boundaries and enables independent deployment. Tech Leads use DDD to reduce coupling and improve team autonomy.

questions.title: What should a module\'s public API vs internal structure look like?
questions.prompt: What should a module\'s public API vs internal structure look like?

options.text: Both approaches are equivalent — expose everything for flexibility
Exposing internals (models, validators, crypto) creates coupling; consumers depend on implementation details that change; a clean public API with use-case-oriented functions hides internals
Internal functions should also be exported for testing
`export type` is TypeScript-only and should be avoided for compatibility

questions.explanation: Leaking internals means consumers couple to `UserModel`, `hashPassword`, etc. If you switch from bcrypt to argon2, all consumers break. Clean API: export only what consumers need (use cases, not mechanisms). For testing internals, use testing-specific exports or test through the public API. Follow the principle of least privilege — expose the minimum needed.

questions.title: What is the dependency injection pattern and why does it improve module testability?
questions.prompt: What is the dependency injection pattern and why does it improve module testability?

options.text: DI makes code more complex without any benefit
DI injects dependencies from outside, enabling mock/stub injection in tests and swapping implementations without changing the class
DI only works with TypeScript decorators
DI requires a DI container framework

questions.explanation: Without DI, `OrderService` is tightly coupled to `PostgresDatabase` and `SendGridEmailer`. Tests would need real DB/email connections. With DI: pass mock objects in tests; swap `PostgresDatabase` for `MongoDB` without changing `OrderService`; the class depends on interfaces (duck typing), not implementations. This is the "D" in SOLID (Dependency Inversion Principle).

questions.title: How should a Tech Lead handle the "utils explosion" anti-pattern?
questions.prompt: How should a Tech Lead handle the "utils explosion" anti-pattern?

options.text: Create a single `utils.js` file with all utility functions

Organize utilities by domain/purpose (`date-utils.js`, `string-utils.js`, `array-utils.js`), ensure each utility is pure and well-tested, and deprecate/delete utilities that duplicate native browser APIs
Avoid all utility functions — inline logic in each component
All utilities should be moved to a separate npm package

questions.explanation: "Utils explosion" — a giant `utils.js` with everything — causes: circular dependencies, poor discoverability, untested code, and duplicating built-in APIs (custom `isEmpty` when `arr.length === 0` suffices). Best practice: domain-organized utils; pure functions (easy to test); named exports (tree-shakeable); regular audit to remove functions now available natively (e.g., custom `flatMap` pre-ES2019). Prefer standard library over custom utilities.

questions.title: What is the tech lead\'s approach to managing breaking changes in an internal shared module?
questions.prompt: What is the tech lead\'s approach to managing breaking changes in an internal shared module?

options.text: Immediately remove deprecated APIs and force all teams to update at once
Use semantic versioning: add new API (minor bump), mark old API as `@deprecated` with migration docs, keep both for 1-2 major versions, then remove in a major version with a migration guide
Never make breaking changes — design all APIs to last forever
Breaking changes should be communicated only in Slack, not in code

questions.explanation: Breaking change management: 1) **Add** new API, **keep** old API. 2) **`@deprecated`** JSDoc with link to replacement. 3) **Minor version** bump. 4) **Communication**: changelog, team announcement, migration guide. 5) After transition period (1-2 major versions), **remove** in major bump. This approach allows teams to migrate at their own pace and avoids "big bang" coordinations. Use `eslint-plugin-deprecation` to surface deprecated usages in CI.

questions.title: A Tech Lead designs a centralized error handling strategy for a Node.js Express API. Which approach is the most robust for production?
questions.prompt: A Tech Lead designs a centralized error handling strategy for a Node.js Express API. Which approach is the most robust for production?

options.text: Option A — inline try/catch is more explicit and easier for junior developers to understand
Option B — centralized error middleware ensures consistent error responses, logging, and status codes across all routes without duplicating error-handling logic
Both are equivalent; the choice is purely stylistic
Option B is dangerous because unhandled errors in `asyncHandler` will crash the server

questions.explanation: Option A scatters error handling across every route, leading to inconsistent formats, missing logging, and high maintenance overhead. A Tech Lead should implement a central error middleware that all routes funnel into via `next(err)`, combined with a typed error hierarchy (`AppError`, `ValidationError`, etc.) to produce structured, consistent API error responses with proper HTTP status codes.

questions.title: What is the right strategy for structuring a typed error hierarchy?
questions.prompt: What is the right strategy for structuring a typed error hierarchy?

options.text: All errors should extend `Error` directly for simplicity

A typed error hierarchy enables structured error handling: catch by type, map to HTTP status codes automatically, distinguish operational from programming errors, and generate consistent API error responses
Typed errors require TypeScript — not possible in vanilla JavaScript

questions.explanation: `isOperational: true` marks expected errors (validation, not found) that should be reported gracefully vs programming bugs (`TypeError`, `ReferenceError`) that should crash the process (or at least alert). The hierarchy enables: `if (error instanceof ValidationError) return res.status(400)`; central error handler that maps error types to responses; consistent error codes for frontend handling; and filtering operational errors from monitoring alerts.

questions.title: How should a Tech Lead implement distributed tracing for errors across microservices?
questions.prompt: How should a Tech Lead implement distributed tracing for errors across microservices?

options.text: Log all errors to `console.error` in each service
